{{Short description|Mathematical constant}}
In [[mathematics]], the '''Glaisher–Kinkelin constant''' or '''Glaisher's constant''', typically denoted {{mvar|A}}, is a [[mathematical constant]], related to [[special functions]] like the [[K-function|{{mvar|K}}-function]] and the [[Barnes G-function|Barnes {{mvar|G}}-function]]. The constant also appears in a number of [[summation|sums]] and [[integral]]s, especially those involving the [[gamma function]] and the [[Riemann zeta function]]. It is named after [[mathematician]]s [[James Whitbread Lee Glaisher]] and [[Hermann Kinkelin]].

Its approximate value is:
:{{mvar|A}} = {{val|1.28242712910062263687}}... &nbsp; {{OEIS|id=A074962}}.

Glaisher's constant plays a role both in mathematics and in [[physics]]. It appears when giving a closed form expression for [[Porter's constant]], when estimating the efficiency of the [[Euclidean algorithm]]. It also is connected to solutions of [[Painlevé transcendents|Painlevé differential equations]] and the [[Gaudin model]].<ref name=":1" />

== Definition ==

The Glaisher–Kinkelin constant {{mvar|A}} can be defined via the following [[Limit (mathematics)|limit]]:<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |last=Weisstein |first=Eric W. |title=Glaisher-Kinkelin Constant |url=https://mathworld.wolfram.com/Glaisher-KinkelinConstant.html |access-date=2024-10-05 |website=mathworld.wolfram.com |language=en}}</ref>
:<math>A=\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty} \frac{H(n)}{n^{\tfrac{n^2}{2}+\tfrac{n}{2}+\tfrac{1}{12}}\,e^{-\tfrac{n^2}{4}}}</math>
where <math>H(n)</math> is the [[hyperfactorial]]:<math display="block">
H(n)= \prod_{i=1}^{n} i^i = 1^1\cdot 2^2\cdot 3^3 \cdot {...}\cdot n^n</math>An analogous limit, presenting a similarity between <math>A</math> and <math>\sqrt{2\pi}</math>, is given by [[Stirling's approximation|Stirling's formula]] as:
:<math>\sqrt{2\pi}=\lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{n!}{n^{n+\frac12}\,e^{-n}}</math>
with<math display="block">
n!= \prod_{i=1}^{n} i = 1 \cdot 2\cdot 3\cdot  {...} \cdot n</math>which shows that just as ''π'' is obtained from approximation of the [[Factorial|factorials]], ''A'' is obtained from the approximation of the hyperfactorials.

== Relation to special functions ==

Just as the factorials can be extended to the [[Complex number|complex numbers]] by the [[gamma function]] such that <math>\Gamma(n)=(n-1)!</math> for positive integers ''n'', the hyperfactorials can be extended by the [[K-function]]<ref>{{Cite web |last=Weisstein |first=Eric W. |title=K-Function |url=https://mathworld.wolfram.com/K-Function.html |access-date=2024-10-05 |website=mathworld.wolfram.com |language=en}}</ref> with <math>K(n)= H(n-1)</math> also for positive integers ''n'', where:

:<math>K(z)=(2\pi)^{-\frac{z-1}2} \exp\left[\binom{z}{2}+\int_0^{z-1} \ln \Gamma(t + 1)\,dt\right]</math>

This gives:<ref name=":1">{{Cite book|author1-link=Steven R. Finch |last=Finch |first=Steven R. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Pl5I2ZSI6uAC |title=Mathematical Constants |date=2003-08-18 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=978-0-521-81805-6 |language=en}}</ref>

:<math>A=\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty} \frac{K(n+1)}{n^{\tfrac{n^2}{2}+\tfrac{n}{2}+\tfrac{1}{12}}\,e^{-\tfrac{n^2}{4}}}</math>.

A related function is the [[Barnes G-function|Barnes {{mvar|G}}-function]] which is given by

:<math>G(n)=\frac{(\Gamma(n))^{n-1}}{K(n)}</math>

and for which a similar limit exists:<ref name=":0" />

:<math>\frac1A=\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty} \frac{G(n+1)}{\left(2\pi\right)^\frac{n}{2} n^{\frac{n^2}{2}-\frac{1}{12}} e^{-\frac{3n^2}{4}+\frac{1}{12}}}</math>.

The Glaisher-Kinkelin constant also appears in the evaluation of the K-function and Barnes-G function at half and quarter [[integer]] values such as:<ref name=":1" /><ref>{{Cite web |last=Weisstein |first=Eric W. |title=Barnes G-Function |url=https://mathworld.wolfram.com/BarnesG-Function.html |access-date=2024-10-05 |website=mathworld.wolfram.com |language=en}}</ref>

:<math>K(1/2) = \frac{A^{3/2}}{2^{1/24}e^{1/8}}</math>

:<math>K(1/4) = A^{9/8}\exp\left(\frac{G}{4\pi}-\frac{3}{32}\right)</math>

:<math>G(1/2) = \frac{2^{1/24}e^{1/8}}{A^{3/2}\pi^{1/4}}</math>

:<math>G(1/4) = \frac{1}{2^{9/16}A^{9/8}\pi^{3/16}\varpi^{3/8}}\exp\left(\frac{3}{32}-\frac{G}{4\pi}\right)</math>

with <math>G</math> being [[Catalan's constant]] and <math>\varpi=\frac{\Gamma(1/4)^2}{2\sqrt{2\pi}}</math> being the [[lemniscate constant]].

Similar to the [[Particular values of the gamma function#Products|gamma function]], there exists a multiplication formula for the K-function. It involves Glaisher's constant:<ref name=":2" />
:<math>\prod_{j=1}^{n-1}K\left(\frac jn \right) = A^{\frac{n^2-1}{n}}n^{-\frac{1}{12n}}e^{\frac{1-n^2}{12n}}</math>

The [[logarithm]] of ''G''(''z'' + 1) has the following [[asymptotic expansion]], as established by Barnes:<ref>[[E. T. Whittaker]] and [[G. N. Watson]], "[[A Course of Modern Analysis]]", CUP.</ref>

: <math>\ln G(z+1) = \frac{z^2}{2} \ln z - \frac{3z^2}{4} + \frac{z}{2}\ln 2\pi -\frac{1}{12} \ln z + \left(\frac{1}{12}-\ln A \right)+\sum_{k=1}^N \frac{B_{2k + 2}}{4k\left(k + 1\right)z^{2k}}+O\left(\frac{1}{z^{2N + 2}}\right)</math>

The Glaisher-Kinkelin constant is related to the derivatives of the [[Euler's constant#Euler-constant function|Euler-constant function]]:<ref name=":2">{{Cite journal |last1=Sondow |first1=Jonathan |last2=Hadjicostas |first2=Petros |date=2006-10-16 |title=The generalized-Euler-constant function <math>\gamma(z)</math> and a generalization of Somos's quadratic recurrence constant |journal=Journal of Mathematical Analysis and Applications |volume=332 |pages=292–314 |doi=10.1016/j.jmaa.2006.09.081 |arxiv=math/0610499 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite arXiv |last1=Pilehrood |first1=Khodabakhsh Hessami |last2=Pilehrood |first2=Tatiana Hessami |date=2008-08-04 |title=Vacca-type series for values of the generalized-Euler-constant function and its derivative |class=math.NT |eprint=0808.0410 |language=en}}</ref>

: <math>\gamma'(-1)= \frac{11}{6}\ln2 + 6\ln A - \frac32 \ln\pi - 1</math>
: <math>\gamma''(-1) = \frac{10}{3}\ln2 + 24\ln A - 4 \ln\pi  - \frac{7\zeta(3)}{2\pi^2}- \frac{13}{4}</math>

<math>A</math> also is related to the [[Lerch transcendent]]:<ref name=":3">{{Cite journal |author1=Jesús Guillera | author1-link=Jesús Guillera |last2=Sondow |first2=Jonathan |date=2008 |title=Double integrals and infinite products for some classical constants via analytic continuations of Lerch's transcendent |journal=The Ramanujan Journal |volume=16 |issue=3 |pages=247–270 |doi=10.1007/s11139-007-9102-0 |arxiv=math/0506319 |issn=1382-4090}}</ref>

:<math>\frac{\partial\Phi}{\partial s}(-1,-1,1)=3\ln A - \frac13\ln2 - \frac 14</math>

Glaisher's constant may be used to give values of the derivative of the [[Riemann zeta function]] as closed form expressions, such as:<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite web |last=Weisstein |first=Eric W. |title=Riemann Zeta Function |url=https://mathworld.wolfram.com/RiemannZetaFunction.html |access-date=2024-10-05 |website=mathworld.wolfram.com |language=en}}</ref>

:<math>\zeta'(-1)=\frac{1}{12}-\ln A</math>

:<math>\zeta'(2)=\frac{\pi^2} 6  \left( \gamma+\ln 2\pi - 12 \ln A \right)</math>

where {{mvar|γ}} is the [[Euler–Mascheroni constant]].

== Series expressions ==

The above formula for <math>\zeta'(2)</math> gives the following series:<ref name=":0" />

:<math>\sum_{k=2}^\infty \frac{\ln k}{k^2}=\frac{\pi^2} 6  \left( 12 \ln A - \gamma-\ln 2\pi \right)</math>

which directly leads to the following product found by [[James Whitbread Lee Glaisher|Glaisher]]:

:<math>\prod_{k=1}^\infty k^\frac{1}{k^2} = \left(\frac{A^{12}}{2\pi e^\gamma} \right)^\frac{\pi^2}{6}</math>

Similarly it is

:<math>\sum_{k\ge 3}^{k\text{ odd}} \frac{\ln k}{k^2}=\frac{\pi^2}{24}  \left( 36  \ln A - 3 \gamma -  \ln 16\pi^3  \right)</math>

which gives:

:<math>\prod_{k\ge 3}^{k\text{ odd}} k^\frac{1}{k^2} = \left(\frac{A^{36}}{16\pi^3 e^{3\gamma}} \right)^\frac{\pi^2}{24}</math>

An alternative product formula, defined over the [[prime numbers]], reads:<ref>{{Cite journal |doi = 10.1142/S1793042112500297|title = Glaisher-Type Products over the Primes|journal = International Journal of Number Theory|volume = 08|issue = 2|pages = 543–550|year = 2012|last1 = Van Gorder|first1 = Robert A. | url=https://stars.library.ucf.edu/facultybib2010/3418 }}</ref>

:<math>\prod_{p \text{ prime}} p^\frac{1}{p^2-1} = \frac{A^{12}}{2\pi e^\gamma}, </math>

Another product is given by:<ref name=":2" />

:<math>\prod_{n=1}^\infty \left(\frac{en^n}{(n+1)^n}\right)^{(-1)^{n-1}} = \frac{2^{1/6} e\sqrt\pi}{A^6} </math>

A series involving the [[cosine integral]] is:<ref>{{cite arXiv |last=Pain |first=Jean-Christophe |title=Series representations for the logarithm of the Glaisher-Kinkelin constant |date=2023-04-15 |class=math.NT |eprint=2304.07629}}</ref>

:<math>\sum_{k=1}^\infty \frac{\text{Ci}(2k\pi)}{k^2}=\frac{\pi^2}{2}(4\ln A -1)</math>

[[Helmut Hasse]] gave another series representation for the logarithm of Glaisher's constant, following from a series for the Riemann zeta function:<ref name=":3">{{Cite journal |author1=Jesús Guillera | author1-link=Jesús Guillera |last2=Sondow |first2=Jonathan |date=2008 |title=Double integrals and infinite products for some classical constants via analytic continuations of Lerch's transcendent |journal=The Ramanujan Journal |volume=16 |issue=3 |pages=247–270 |doi=10.1007/s11139-007-9102-0 |arxiv=math/0506319 |issn=1382-4090}}</ref>

:<math>\ln A=\frac 1 8 - \frac 1 2  \sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac 1 {n+1} \sum_{k=0}^n (-1)^k \binom n k (k+1)^2 \ln(k+1)</math>

==Integrals==

The following are some definite integrals involving Glaisher's constant:<ref name=":1" />

:<math>\int_0^\infty \frac{x \ln x}{e^{2 \pi x}-1} \, dx = \frac 1 {24}-\frac 1 2 \ln A</math>

:<math>\int_0^\frac12 \ln\Gamma(x) \, dx = \frac 3 2 \ln A+\frac 5 {24} \ln 2+\frac 1 4 \ln \pi</math>

the latter being a special case of:<ref>{{cite arXiv |last=Adamchik |first=V. S. |title=Contributions to the Theory of the Barnes Function |date=2003-08-08 |eprint=math/0308086 }}</ref>

:<math> \int_0^z \ln \Gamma(x)\,dx=\frac{z(1-z)}{2}+\frac{z}{2}\ln 2\pi +z\ln\Gamma(z) -\ln G(1+z) </math>
A double integral is given by:<ref name=":3" />

:<math>\int_0^1 \int_0^1 \frac{-x}{(1+xy)^2\ln xy}dxdy= 6\ln A - \frac16 \ln 2 - \frac12 \ln\pi  - \frac12</math>

==Generalizations==

The Glaisher-Kinkelin constant can be viewed as the first constant in a sequence of infinitely many so-called ''generalized Glaisher constants'' or ''Bendersky constants''.<ref name=":1" /> They emerge from studying the following product:<math display="block">
\prod_{m=1}^{n} m^{m^k} = 1^{1^k} \cdot 2^{2^k}\cdot 3^{3^k}\cdot  {...} \cdot n^{n^k}</math>Setting <math>k = 0</math> gives the factorial <math>n!</math>, while choosing <math>k = 1</math> gives the hyperfactorial <math>H(n)</math>.

Defining the following function<math display="block">P_k(n) = \left(\frac{n^{k+1}}{k+1}+\frac{n^k}{2}+\frac{B_{k+1}}{k+1}\right)\ln n - \frac{n^{k+1}}{(k+1)^2}+k!\sum_{j=1}^{k-1} \frac{B_{j+1}}{(j+1)!}\frac{n^{k-j}}{(k-j)!}\left(\ln n + \sum_{i=1}^j \frac{1}{k-i+1}\right)</math>with the [[Bernoulli number|Bernoulli numbers]] <math>B_k</math> (and using <math>B_1=0</math>), one may approximate the above products asymptotically via <math>\exp({P_k(n)})</math>.

For <math>k = 0</math> we get Stirling's approximation without the factor <math>\sqrt{2\pi}</math> as <math>\exp({P_0(n)})=n^{n+\frac12} e^{-n}</math>.

For <math>k = 1</math> we obtain <math>\exp({P_1(n)})=n^{\tfrac{n^2}{2}+\tfrac{n}{2}+\tfrac{1}{12}}\,e^{-\tfrac{n^2}{4}}</math>, similar as in the limit definition of <math>A</math>.

This leads to the following definition of the generalized Glaisher constants:

:<math> A_k:=\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty} \left( e^{-P_k(n)} \prod_{m=1}^{n} m^{m^k}\right) </math>

which may also be written as:

:<math> \ln A_k:=\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty} \left(-P_k(n)+\sum_{m=1}^{n} {m^k}\ln m\right) </math>
This gives <math>A_0=\sqrt{2\pi}</math> and <math>A_1=A</math> and in general:<ref name=":1" /><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Choudhury |first=Bejoy K. |date=1995 |title=The Riemann Zeta-Function and Its Derivatives |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/52768 |journal= Proceedings of the Royal Society of London A |volume=450 |issue=1940 |pages=477–499 |doi=10.1098/rspa.1995.0096 |jstor=52768 |bibcode=1995RSPSA.450..477C |issn=0962-8444|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Adamchik |first=Victor S. |date=1998-12-21 |title=Polygamma functions of negative order |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0377042798001927 |journal=Journal of Computational and Applied Mathematics |volume=100 |issue=2 |pages=191–199 |doi=10.1016/S0377-0427(98)00192-7 |issn=0377-0427|url-access=subscription }}</ref>
:<math> A_k=\exp\left(\frac{B_{k+1}}{k+1}H_k-\zeta'(-k)\right) </math>
with the [[Harmonic number|harmonic numbers]] <math>H_k</math> and <math>H_0=0</math>. 

Because of the formula
:<math> \zeta'(-2m)=(-1)^m \frac{(2m)!}{2(2\pi)^{2m}}\zeta(2m+1) </math>
for <math>m > 0</math>, there exist closed form expressions for <math>A_{k}</math> with even <math>k=2m</math> in terms of the [[Particular values of the Riemann zeta function|values of the Riemann zeta function]] such as:<ref name=":1" />

:<math>A_2=\exp\left(\frac{\zeta(3)}{4\pi^2}\right)</math>

:<math>A_4=\exp\left(-\frac{3\zeta(5)}{4\pi^4}\right)</math>

For odd <math>k=2m-1</math> one can express the constants <math>A_{k}</math> in terms of the derivative of the Riemann zeta function such as:

:<math>A_1=\exp\left(-\frac{\zeta'(2)}{2\pi^2}+\frac{\gamma+\ln2\pi}{12}\right)</math>

:<math>A_3=\exp\left(\frac{3\zeta'(4)}{4\pi^4}-\frac{\gamma+\ln2\pi}{120}\right)</math>
